title: Expansion of the universe
description: Increase in distance between parts of the universe
wiki_lead:
The expansion of the universe is the increase in distance between gravitationally unbound parts of the observable universe with time. It is an intrinsic expansion, so it does not mean that the universe expands into anything or that space exists outside it. To any observer in the universe, it appears that all but the nearest galaxies (which are bound to each other by gravity) move away at speeds that are proportional to their distance from the observer, on average. While objects cannot move faster than light, this limitation applies only with respect to local reference frames and does not limit the recession rates of cosmologically distant objects.
The expansion of the universe was discovered by separate theoretical and observational work in the 1920s. Since then, the expansion has become a core aspect of the astrophysical field of cosmology. Many major scientific projects have sought to characterize the expansion and understand its effects.
Cosmic expansion is a key feature of Big Bang cosmology. Within the theory of general relativity, it is modeled mathematically with the Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker (FLRW) metric. The consensus or "standard" model of cosmology, the Lambda-CDM model, hypothesizes different expansion rates during different times, depending on the physical properties of the contents of spacetime. The very earliest expansion, called inflation, saw the universe suddenly expand by a factor of at least 1026 in every direction within about 10−32 seconds. Cosmic expansion subsequently decelerated to much slower rates, until around 9.8 billion years after the Big Bang (4 billion years ago) it began to gradually expand more quickly, and is still doing so. Physicists have postulated the existence of dark energy, appearing as a cosmological constant in the simplest gravitational models, as a way to explain this late-time acceleration which is predicted to be dominant in the future.
The concept of the expansion of the universe is difficult to explain, leading to several misconceptions about its nature, origin, and effects.

History of the concept
In 1912–1914, Vesto Slipher discovered that light from remote galaxies was redshifted, a phenomenon later interpreted as galaxies receding from the Earth. In 1922, Alexander Friedmann used the Einstein field equations to provide theoretical evidence that the universe is expanding.
The key astronomical demonstration of the expansion of the universe is known as Hubble's law or sometimes as the Hubble–Lemaître law. The name and thus the honor of the discovery has been debated. In 1924, Swedish astronomer Knut Lundmark found observational evidence for expansion. While his results were reasonably accurate even by today's standards, they relied upon galaxy diameter measurements and  the distance to the Andromeda Galaxy which were unproven at the time.
In 1927, Georges Lemaître derived solutions for Einstein's equations of general relativity and applied them to data published by Slipher and Hubble
grok_lead: The expansion of the universe is the ongoing increase in the scale of space, causing distant galaxies to recede from one another at speeds proportional to their distance, as quantified by Hubble's law (v = Hâd, where v is recession velocity, d is distance, and Hâ is the Hubble constant). This relationship is observed through the redshift of light from distant galaxies, where light stretches to longer wavelengths due to the expansion of space itself, which occurs uniformly in all directions with no central point. This phenomenon, a cornerstone of modern cosmology, originated from the Big Bang approximately 13.8 billion years ago and is evidenced by the cosmological redshift of light from remote objects, where expanding space stretches wavelengths toward the red end of the spectrum. Initially, the expansion decelerated due to gravitational attraction from matter, but around 9 billion years after the Big Bang, it began accelerating, driven by the mysterious force known as dark energy, which comprises about 68-70% of the universe 's total energy content. Edwin Hubble's groundbreaking observations in 1929 provided the first empirical evidence for this expansion, using Cepheid variable stars to measure distances to "nebulae" (now known as galaxies) and spectroscopy to detect their redshifts, demonstrating that the universe is not static but dynamically enlarging. Earlier theoretical foundations were laid by Alexander Friedmann in 1922 and Georges LemaÃ®tre in 1927, who derived expanding universe models from Einstein's general relativity, with LemaÃ®tre proposing a "primeval atom" akin to the Big Bang. The current expansion rate, or Hubble constant, is estimated at around 70 km/s/Mpc based on data from missions like the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP) and the Hubble Space Telescope, with values ranging from about 67 to 73 km/s/Mpc due to the ongoing Hubble tension between early-universe and local measurements, though precise resolution remains a topic of active refinement. The acceleration of expansion was discovered in 1998 through observations of Type Ia supernovae by teams led by Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt, and Adam Riess, who found these "standard candle" explosions appearing fainter and more distant than expected in a decelerating universe, earning them the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics. This revelation implies that dark energy dominates the universe 's fate, potentially leading to an ever-accelerating " Big Rip " or continued dilution, though its exact natureâpossibly vacuum energy or a dynamic field called quintessenceâremains unknown. Early in cosmic history, a brief phase of rapid expansion called inflation occurred fractions of a second after the Big Bang, stretching the universe exponentially and smoothing out irregularities to explain its observed flatness and uniformity on large scales. Ongoing missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope, Euclid, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope continue to probe these dynamics, refining our understanding of the universe 's composition (roughly 5% ordinary matter, 25% dark matter, and 70% dark energy) and evolution.
